paras.t: Question 01.1 was well answered, with students generally having a really secure understanding the characteristics of the drainage basin.
Question 01.2, 04.2 and 06.2 were very accessible. Students coped with these graphically based questions, identifying patterns, manipulating data and picking out anomalies in support.

Question 02.3 and 05.3 produced very strong responses, though novel situation questions are generally an area for improvement as they require students to think on their feet under the pressure of the exam, clearly quite a challenging task given the time available.
The 9-mark AO1/AO2 questions in Section C produced similar outcomes, though question 06.4 was a little stronger more generally.

Question 01.4 performed better than expected this year. The vast majority of students understood that deforestation was a major factor driving change in the magnitude of carbon stores. With some development, this factor alone produced generally clear answers.
Question 05.5 generally performed well once students understood the concept of human occupation and provided this was backed up with an appropriate case study of a multi hazardous environment.
Question 05.1 about island arc formation produced a very polarised set of responses. Too many confused arcs with chains which have very different theories around their formation.

Question 02.2 required students to analyse map data. Students needed to look at patterns, use supporting data, and identify anomalies. There were also opportunities to cross reference between the two maps, particularly in ascertaining the extent of correlation between rainfall and temperature.

Some students found Question 03.2 on the coastal unit quite challenging. However, it was perhaps a little more simplistic than many realised. It showed three variables: different sea level change scenarios; no and maximum human response in the management of sea level changes and how these two variables affect potential impacts of sea level rise. Those that understood this information readily achieved the highest marks once they picked out patterns, anomalies and used some data in support.

Question 03.3 did not really perform too well in novel situations. Students needed to assess the sustainability of different approaches to coastal management. It was much more simplistic than many realised. It did not require any detailed knowledge of the named approaches or case study recital. It was simply about showing understanding that some approaches (e.g. working with nature through soft engineering) are generally considered more sustainable than others (e.g. hard engineering). There was also some debate to be had around ideas of managed retreat in terms of its sustainability.

Question 03.4 was very much a physical essay question. Too many brought in material which simply was not relevant to this question. The only real route to bringing in coastal management was through developing ideas of unintended consequences of management further down the coast e.g. by starving beaches of sediment and accelerating erosion elsewhere.

Question 01.1 (AO1) (4 marks) was generally well done by students. Examiners allowed a multitude of approaches including a more systems-based approach as well as outlining features and characteristics. It was pleasing to note just how many students made relevant points about these features. ‘Max’ is used when the student could score more marks but has reached the maximum available.

On Question 03.1 (AO1) (4 marks) understanding the sequence in the formation of such landforms is very important on these four-mark questions. The student should have started with a beach, the tidal range and an onshore wind, before moving on to dune stabilisation by vegetation.

In Question 01.2 (AO3) (6 marks) it’s evident that students are now well used to working with data, interpreting map information and analysis using data to support. The key to success was in understanding that this was a compound, cumulative bar graph showing how global emissions are predicted to fall by 2030. There was plenty to analyse here including the identification of Turkey and Mexico as obvious anomalies. Whilst there is never any credit for applying knowledge, this question did allow students to note that generally richer more developing counties were forecast to make bigger contributions to the reduction in greenhouse gases. This was because such information was hinted at in the resources through reference to G20 and non-G20 countries.

On question 03.2 (AO3) (6 marks), once students understood the three variables in the response it became relatively straightforward to access Level 2 and full marks. Even where there was minor misunderstanding, access to Level 2 was still possible.

Question 04.2 (AO3) (6 marks) there were many ways to access credit by spotting the differences between and within north and interior Alaska. Students who drifted into applying knowledge and understanding failed to score credit for such an approach.

In question 05.2 (AO3) (6 marks) students needed to compare patterns on the map with information evidence in the resource. There was plenty to write in terms of the quite varied patterns on the map and how this correlated or arguably contradicted that which was evident in the resource. There was ample opportunity to evaluate the effectiveness of the resource. This is always creditable on the skills questions. In this case, the logarithmic scale was really of quite limited use in displaying what is clearly a very large variation in risk of seismic event in this part of the USA.

In question 06.3 (AO1 & AO2) (9 marks) a simplified nutrient cycle was displayed. Students needed to consider how human activity might affect different aspects of both the stores and transfers. The best responses showed how knock-on effects could occur within the cycle once one part is disrupted.

In question 01.3 (AO1 & AO2) (6 marks) there was no real credit for long narrative on either sustainable water supply case study material or on a flooding case study. This was not the focus of the question. Students had to pick out physical and human factors affecting the water cycle, many of which were hinted at in the resource. Once they did this, the question then needed some consideration of the relative importance i.e. which group of factors was more important in meeting the definition provided in the resource. Students were free to argue either way. Some suggested that without a supply of water in the first place, sustainability would be impossible to achieve. Others argued that it does not matter how much water is available, if it is not potable water, it can never be sustainable.

Question 03.3 (AO1 & AO2) (6 marks), the coasts question, focused on different groups and types of coastal management strategies, many of which would be familiar to students. The resource was set out as a series of steps in an integrated approach. Students needed to consider each step and judge or assess the likely sustainability of the approach. For example, hard engineering schemes certainly perform a function in protecting a coastline. However, many argue that these are not in keeping the local environment and may disruption natural processes, causing issues elsewhere. Conversely many would argue that restoring wetlands is inherently sustainable as coastal impacts can be absorbed by the wetlands, whilst also creating natural habitats supporting a rejuvenated ecosystem.

On question 04.3 (AO1 & AO2) (6 marks) an infographic was presented which displayed a variety of changes to alpine tundra in the coming decades in different climate change scenarios. Students had to translate those changes into potential impacts. The focus was then on picking out the potential negative impacts or challenges. Opportunities were missed to consider impacts on farming, tourism, water supply and invasive species into the natural habitats.

Question 06.4 (AO1 & AO2) (9 marks) required consideration of the likely impacts of climate change on savanna grasslands, with a particularly focus upon people. So, whilst climate change initially affects the natural environment, it was the knock-on effects to people which really triggered the credit.

Question 05.4 (AO1 & AO2) (9 mark) should have been more straightforward than many found this to be. A typical answer acknowledged that economic development will usually mean that a higher income country will usually have more tools at its disposal to tackle wildfire both in planning for and responding to it. A combination of education, land use mapping, satellite imagery including weather forecasting can also help to plan for a wildfire. Wide ranging responses are also more readily available in richer parts of the world through deployment of firefighters, using aerial techniques and controlled burning. The nuance of the question really invited students to draw on their own case study support to show how other factors may contribute more substantially. This included consideration of drought, availability of fuel and proximity to built-up areas. Indeed, some of the worst wildfires (in terms of impact on people) have been in some of the richest parts of the world.
On question 01.4, students did analyse a number of factors driving change in the magnitude of carbon stores.
For Question 05.5 (AO1 & AO2) (20 marks) provided students had a suitable case study and understood the meaning of the term human occupation, many went on to produce clear, strong responses.

Weaker answers on question 03.4 (AO1 & AO2) (20 marks) really failed to understand the context of the question i.e. that the focus was on high energy, erosional coastlines. They were then expected to consider factors creating such environments i.e. marine factors (fetch, tides, currents, destructive waves, deep water coastlines) alongside sub aerial factors (weather, low pressure and associated impacts), as well as rock type and geology.
Question 04.4 (AO1 & AO2) (20 marks) the focus was often in the right area, but the answers lacked depth.

On question 04.4 (AO1 & AO2) (20 marks), whilst the focus was in the correct area i.e. the Lake District, the argument was limited, and it never really got the required depth to produce a clear answer. The relative brevity also contributed to that lack of depth.

7037/1 followed an identical structure to previous papers. Students are well used to this approach, given the age of the specification. Whilst it remains a challenging paper, it differentiated well and those who prepared thoroughly had every chance to access the full range of marks. It was really pleasing to see a very equitable performance across the optional units of Section B and Section C. This meant that whatever the route through the paper, students had an equal chance of success.
Four-mark questions performed well, provided the students had the appropriate level of understanding of the specification content.
In general, analysis and interpretation of map evidence requires further development.

4-mark questions are point marked. A mark may be awarded where a student makes a single relevant point and subsequent marks awarded (if applicable) where the student develops those points with additional knowledge.

6-mark, 9-mark and 20-mark questions are levels marked where the response is holistically marked against the assessment objectives, given a mid-level mark initially and then a fine tune mark awarded within that level.
AO1: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of places, environments, concepts, processes, interactions and change, at a variety of scales (30-40%).
AO2: Apply knowledge and understanding in different contexts to interpret, analyse and evaluate geographical information and issues (30-40%).
AO3: Use a variety of relevant quantitative, qualitative and fieldwork skills to:
- investigate geographical questions and issues - interpret, analyse and evaluate data and evidence - construct arguments and draw conclusions (20-30%)
